value_text: 25–30 °C: optimum range of the intrinsic rate of population growth (r) at constant laboratory temperatures. Immature development was fastest at 30 °C (development optimum 29.7 °C; lower development threshold 10.4 °C).
context: Ae. albopictus, F2 laboratory population from La Réunion (Indian Ocean, tropical origin). Eight constant temperatures (5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40 °C). Traits: immature development, survival, longevity, fecundity, gonotrophic cycle.
quote: optimum intrinsic rate of growth (r) was observed between 25 and 30 degrees C
citation: Delatte H, Gimonneau G, Triboire A, Fontenille D. Influence of temperature on immature development, survival, longevity, fecundity, and gonotrophic cycles of Aedes albopictus, vector of chikungunya and dengue in the Indian Ocean. J Med Entomol. 2009;46(1):33–41.
notes: Number confirmed, context slightly different: in the source 25–30 °C is the optimum of the population growth rate r (development + survival + fecundity combined), not of development alone; the development optimum is 29.7 °C. Constant lab temperatures and a tropical population; field temperatures fluctuate. Suggested wording: '25–30 °C: optimal range for population growth in the laboratory'. Supporting lab study with a temperate population (Trento, northern Italy; tested 10, 15, 25, 30 °C): Marini G et al. Insects 2020;11(11):808, doi:10.3390/insects11110808 — adult longevity and fecundity were substantially greater at 25 °C; larvae developed even at 10 and 15 °C, but no blood-feeding was observed at those low temperatures. Full text of Delatte et al. is paywalled; values taken from the PubMed abstract.

value_text: 26.5 °C (95% CrI 25.3–28.1): temperature of peak predicted hourly female biting (host-seeking) density in urban outdoor field sites. 16.4–37.1 °C: temperatures at which the predicted female biting density was ≥ 1 per person per hour.

numbers.range_definition: predicted female biting density >= 1 per person per hour

context: Field-based study, Guangzhou (southern China, subtropical), urban outdoor sites, Nov 2016–Nov 2017 and June–July 2018. Mosquitoes collected hourly with human-baited double net traps, with site-specific temperature, relative humidity, illuminance and wind speed. Bayesian negative binomial regression; 26.5 °C is the peak of the fitted curve.
quote: female biting was 16.4–37.1 °C, peaking at 26.5 °C (95% credible interval: 25.3–28.1)
citation: Yin Q, Li L, Guo X, Wu R, Shi B, Wang Y, et al. A field-based modeling study on ecological characterization of hourly host-seeking behavior and its associated climatic variables in Aedes albopictus. Parasit Vectors. 2019;12:474.
notes: All numbers confirmed (abstract and results). The 16.4–37.1 °C range is NOT an activity or survival limit: it is the range in which the model predicts at least 1 biting female per person per hour (for males: 21.7–37.1 °C). Hourly (short-term) relation with air temperature, not a seasonal or climatic threshold. Subtropical population; a temperate (European/Greek) population may differ. Same study: predicted density increased with relative humidity and generally decreased with wind speed.

value_text: 9 °C minimum air temperature: threshold for the END of seasonal adult (host-seeking) activity in autumn. Seasonal emergence in spring started above a minimum temperature of 13 °C.
context: Ae. albopictus host-seeking females, BG-Sentinel trap sampling, April–November 2008, Arco and Riva del Garda (Trentino, northern Italy, temperate). One area, one season.
quote: end of adult activity was found at a minimum temperature of 9°C
citation: Roiz D, Rosà R, Arnoldi D, Rizzoli A. Effects of temperature and rainfall on the activity and dynamics of host-seeking Aedes albopictus females in northern Italy. Vector Borne Zoonotic Dis. 2010;10(8):811–816.
notes: The 9 °C is confirmed, but (a) it refers to MINIMUM temperature, not mean temperature, and (b) it marks the end of the seasonal activity period in the trap data, not a general 'strongly reduced activity' level. Suggested wording: 'minimum temperature below ~9 °C: end of the adult activity season (field, northern Italy)'. Full text is paywalled; the averaging period of the minimum temperature could not be checked. Related model parameter: Medlock et al. 2006 (as described in Caminade et al. 2012, doi:10.1098/rsif.2012.0138) put autumn egg diapause at 9.5 °C together with a 13.5 h photoperiod, and spring hatching at 10.5 °C and 11.25 h. Lab (temperate population): no blood-feeding observed at 10 and 15 °C (Marini et al. 2020, doi:10.3390/insects11110808).

value_text: January mean temperature above 0 °C: the widely used threshold for survival of overwintering (diapausing) eggs. In Trentino, a 0 °C January land-surface-temperature threshold, together with 11 °C annual mean, best predicted where the species occurs.
context: Province of Trento, northern Italy (alpine valleys); ovitrap presence/absence vs MODIS land surface temperature (LST) 2001–2009 and human population data; thresholds chosen as those that best fitted the field records. The 0 °C air-temperature criterion itself goes back to Knudsen et al. 1996 and Medlock et al. 2006.
quote: An air temperature of 0°C is the generally accepted threshold for JanTmean
citation: Roiz D, Neteler M, Castellani C, Arnoldi D, Rizzoli A. Climatic factors driving invasion of the tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus) into new areas of Trentino, northern Italy. PLoS One. 2011;6(4):e14800.
notes: Roiz et al. link January mean temperature to the survival of diapausing eggs and cite Knudsen et al. 1996 and Medlock et al. 2006 for the 0 °C value; their own best threshold was 0 °C in LST (land surface temperature), which they consider equivalent to the 0 °C air-temperature threshold. Earliest accessible statement: Knudsen AB, Romi R, Majori G. J Am Mosq Control Assoc 1996;12(2 Pt 1):177–183 (PubMed 8827590; no DOI): winter monthly mean of 0 °C among 'well-established criteria'. Variants: Kobayashi et al. 2002 (Japan) used January mean > −2 °C; Medlock et al. 2006 (as reported by Caminade et al. 2012) treated Jan < 0 °C with rain < 500 mm as highly unsuitable and Jan > 2 °C with rain > 700 mm as totally suitable; the ECDC 2009 model (also via Caminade et al. 2012) ramps from zero suitability below −1 °C to maximum above 3 °C. NOT a lethal limit: in the lab, diapausing eggs of a European strain still hatched after −10 °C for 12–24 h (Thomas SM et al. Parasit Vectors 2012;5:100, doi:10.1186/1756-3305-5-100). Medlock et al. 2006 full text is paywalled and was not read directly.

value_text: Annual mean temperature above 11 °C: distribution threshold derived from the northern range limit in Japan; confirmed as best predictor (with January 0 °C) in Trentino.
context: Larval surveillance in 26 urban and rural areas of the Tohoku district, northern Honshu, Japan, 1998–2000, combined with GIS climatology; the conditions that accounted for the observed northern distribution limit (38–40° N).
quote: an annual mean temperature higher than 11 degrees C
citation: Kobayashi M, Nihei N, Kurihara T. Analysis of northern distribution of Aedes albopictus (Diptera: Culicidae) in Japan by geographical information system. J Med Entomol. 2002;39(1):4–11.
notes: Confirmed in Kobayashi et al. 2002 (same study: January mean > −2 °C, > 186 days per year above 11 °C, > 1,350 degree-days above 11 °C). Roiz et al. 2011 (PLoS One 6:e14800, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0014800) found that the 11 °C annual-mean threshold (in LST), with January 0 °C, gave the best predictors in Trentino, and cite Kobayashi for it. Caminade et al. 2012 (J R Soc Interface 9(75):2708–2717, doi:10.1098/rsif.2012.0138; co-authored by Medlock) use Kobayashi-based bands: > 12 °C totally suitable, 11–12 high, 10–11 moderate, 9–10 low. The attribution to Medlock et al. 2006 could not be checked directly (paywalled). It is a distribution threshold, not a survival limit.

value_text: At least 500 mm (50 cm) mean annual rainfall: long-standing expert criterion for areas where the species can establish, justified by the maintenance of larval habitats. The species is also found in drier areas.
context: Proposed for projecting the European range after the 1990s invasion of Italy, together with a winter monthly mean of 0 °C and a summer mean of about 20 °C. The same paper lists Greece among countries whose climate meets these criteria.
quote: where at least 50 cm of mean annual rainfall occurs
citation: Knudsen AB, Romi R, Majori G. Occurrence and spread in Italy of Aedes albopictus, with implications for its introduction into other parts of Europe. J Am Mosq Control Assoc. 1996;12(2 Pt 1):177–183.
notes: Expert criterion, not a statistically fitted threshold. Roiz et al. 2011 (doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0014800) state that annual precipitation conditions the maintenance of larval habitats, that 500 mm is the significant threshold value (citing Knudsen 1996, Mitchell 1995 and Eritja et al. 2005), but that the species is also found in areas with lower precipitation; they list southern Greece among areas where rainfall may be limiting. Mitchell CJ, J Vector Ecol 1995;20:44–58, is not online and was not read. Variants (as reported by Caminade et al. 2012, doi:10.1098/rsif.2012.0138): Medlock et al. 2006 > 700 mm totally suitable for overwintering, < 500 mm (with January < 0 °C) highly unsuitable; ECDC 2009 model: zero suitability below 450 mm, maximum above 800 mm. Caution for Greece: the species is established in many Greek regional units (Badieritakis E et al. Parasitol Res 2018;117:453–460, doi:10.1007/s00436-017-5721-6), including Attiki (listed by Adeleke et al. 2022), so the 500 mm value should not be used as a hard exclusion in urban areas, where containers and irrigation supply water.

value_text: 90–800 mm cumulative rainfall over the previous 35 days: favourable range for larval (L3–L4) abundance in an empirical model; best together with a 42-day mean minimum temperature above 21 °C.
context: Réunion Island (tropical, Indian Ocean), five sites, 2012–2013; response = mean number of L3 and L4 larvae per trap; empirical Support Vector Regression model chosen from 531 climate indices (32 Météo-France stations); compared with a process-based (ODE) model.
quote: between 90 and 800 mm of rain accumulation over the last 35 days
citation: Tran A, Mangeas M, Demarchi M, Roux E, Degenne P, Haramboure M, et al. Complementarity of empirical and process-based approaches to modelling mosquito population dynamics with Aedes albopictus as an example—Application to the development of an operational mapping tool of vector populations. PLoS One. 2020;15(1):e0227407.
notes: Numbers and window confirmed. The results sentence says larval numbers decrease 'beyond 90 mm or over 800 mm' — read as outside the 90–800 mm range (the lower bound wording looks like a slip in the paper). Transferability to Greece is low: tropical island with very wet areas (the paper mentions areas with > 4000 mm/year) and a different season structure. In dry Greek summers the 90 mm/35-day lower bound would rarely be met, although adults are then abundant, so do not apply it literally.

value_text: Above 800 mm in the previous 35 days: predicted larval numbers stay low (no more than 20 per trap) even when temperature is favourable; authors attribute the negative effect of heavy rain to flushing of immature stages from breeding containers.
context: Same empirical model as item 7 (Réunion Island, L3–L4 larvae per trap, Support Vector Regression).
quote: above 800 mm [...] the predicted number of larvae does not exceed 20
citation: Tran A, Mangeas M, Demarchi M, Roux E, Degenne P, Haramboure M, et al. Complementarity of empirical and process-based approaches to modelling mosquito population dynamics with Aedes albopictus as an example—Application to the development of an operational mapping tool of vector populations. PLoS One. 2020;15(1):e0227407.
notes: The flushing / flooding of oviposition sites is the authors' explanation, not something measured in the study. In Greece 800 mm in 35 days is an extreme amount, so this upper limit would almost never apply. Field evidence on short-term rain effects in Europe is mixed: in northern Italy, rainfall accumulated over 1–4 weeks before sampling was negatively correlated with host-seeking female abundance (Roiz et al. 2010, doi:10.1089/vbz.2009.0098), whereas in Montpellier cumulated rainfall six weeks before sampling was positively associated with abundance (Bartholomée et al. 2025, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0335793).

value_text: About 75–80% relative humidity: typical insectary / laboratory rearing setting (e.g. 75 ± 2% at 27 ± 2 °C; 80 ± 3%). A husbandry condition, not a field threshold or optimum.
context: Marini et al. 2020: laboratory colony from Trento (northern Italy), experiments at 10, 15, 25 and 30 °C, RH fixed at 80 ± 3%, photoperiod 12:12. Damiens et al. 2019: Réunion strain, climate-controlled insectary for SIT mass rearing, 27 ± 2 °C, RH 75 ± 2%, 12L:12D.
quote: RH was controlled and fixed at 80 ± 3%
citation: Marini G, Manica M, Arnoldi D, Inama E, Rosà R, Rizzoli A. Influence of temperature on the life-cycle dynamics of Aedes albopictus population established at temperate latitudes: a laboratory experiment. Insects. 2020;11(11):808.
notes: Second source: Damiens D, Marquereau L, Lebon C, Le Goff G, Gaudillat B, Habchi-Hanriot N, Gouagna LC. Adult medium mass rearing for SIT program development. Insects. 2019;10(8):246, doi:10.3390/insects10080246, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723893/ — insectary at 'RH: 75 ± 2%'. Rearing humidity is chosen for convenience and differs between labs; it is not evidence that the species needs 75–80% RH outdoors. Field relations with RH are inconsistent: hourly host-seeking density increased with RH in Guangzhou (Yin et al. 2019), while presence and abundance were negatively correlated with RH in bivariate analyses in Montpellier (Bartholomée et al. 2025). Do not use as a suitability threshold.

value_text: Annual median absolute humidity above about 10 g/m³: probability of presence increases (no upper threshold found), in a global distribution model; same response for Ae. albopictus and Ae. aegypti.

numbers.variable: annual median absolute humidity (ERA reanalysis, Tetens conversion)

context: Global presence records of Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus; ensemble of boosted regression trees (MaxEnt dropped from the final ensemble), about 5 km resolution. Accessibility, absolute humidity and annual minimum temperature were the strongest predictors.
quote: increased probability of presence with values above 10 g/m3
citation: Dickens BL, Sun H, Jit M, Cook AR, Carrasco LR. Determining environmental and anthropogenic factors which explain the global distribution of Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus. BMJ Glob Health. 2018;3(4):e000801.
notes: Confirmed. Correlative global model (response curve), not a physiological limit; the authors note neither species showed an upper threshold. Kraemer et al. 2015 (eLife 4:e08347, doi:10.7554/eLife.08347) did NOT use humidity: their covariates were temperature suitability, minimum and maximum precipitation, EVI (mean and range) and urbanicity (for Ae. albopictus, temperature suitability contributed 44.3%). Same Dickens model: Ae. albopictus presence probability increased where annual minimum temperature is at least about 2 °C (versus 8 °C for Ae. aegypti).

value_text: Mean wind speed over the 5 weeks before sampling: no effect between 3.7 and 4.3 m/s, negative correlation with abundance above 4.3 m/s (one city). In a European niche model, wind speed lowered predicted habitat suitability; the '4 m/s' value attributed to that model is not stated in its text.

numbers.variable: mean wind speed, sampling day to 5 weeks before

context: Montpellier, France, May–October 2023; adults trapped with BG-Pro traps (lure + CO2) in parks, residential and highly impervious areas; random forest regression on abundance after bivariate GLMM screening.
quote: no effect on abundance between 3.7 m/s and 4.3 m/s, but [...] negative correlation beyond
citation: Bartholomée C, Taconet P, Mercat M, Grail C, Bouhsira E, Fournet F, Moiroux N. Investigating the role of urban vegetation alongside other environmental variables in shaping Aedes albopictus presence and abundance in Montpellier, France. PLoS One. 2025;20(11):e0335793.
notes: 4.3 m/s confirmed (Bartholomée et al. 2025). The '4 m/s' figure is attributed by Bartholomée et al. to Adeleke ED, Shittu RA, Beierkuhnlein C, Thomas SM. High wind speed prevents the establishment of the disease vector mosquito Aedes albopictus in its climatic niche in Europe. Front Environ Sci. 2022;10:846243, doi:10.3389/fenvs.2022.846243 — but no explicit 4 m/s threshold was found in Adeleke's text. Adeleke (MaxEnt, ERA5 10-m annual mean wind) reports that wind speed has a negative effect on predicted habitat suitability and that climatically suitable areas without the species had higher wind speed (3.12 ± 0.04 m/s) than areas where it is established (2.54 ± 0.04 m/s); most established areas had 1.5–4.5 m/s, and Attiki and Lakonia (Greece) are listed among areas with established or introduced populations despite > 4.5 m/s. Hourly scale: host-seeking density generally decreased with wind speed in Guangzhou (Yin et al. 2019; observed 0–7.9 m/s, mean 0.9). Hourly, 5-week and annual 10-m reanalysis wind are different variables and their values are not interchangeable. Closest verified value: 4.3 m/s (5-week mean, one city, one season).

value_text: Percentage of low vegetation (< 3 m) within 250 m of traps: positive (moderate) association with adult abundance in one city; urban vegetation had only a limited effect on presence.
context: Montpellier, France, May–October 2023, BG-Pro traps in urban parks, residential areas and the impervious city centre; land cover from a 0.5 m harmonised map (Pléiades imagery, LiDAR, Urban Atlas); random forest; the average patch size of low vegetation was the top predictor of abundance.
quote: low vegetation cover within a 250 m radius around traps moderately increased abundance
citation: Bartholomée C, Taconet P, Mercat M, Grail C, Bouhsira E, Fournet F, Moiroux N. Investigating the role of urban vegetation alongside other environmental variables in shaping Aedes albopictus presence and abundance in Montpellier, France. PLoS One. 2025;20(11):e0335793.
notes: Single city, single season, correlative model; 'low vegetation' is defined by height (< 3 m) on a specific map product, so the percentage depends on the map used. Associated with abundance, not with presence.

value_text: 10–23% low-vegetation cover within 250 m: range over which the effect on abundance was positive; above 23% no further observable effect (plateau, not decline).
context: Same study as item 12 (Montpellier 2023, random forest partial effect; the fourth most important contributor to abundance).
quote: positive effect between 10% and 23%, beyond which it had no observable effect
citation: Bartholomée C, Taconet P, Mercat M, Grail C, Bouhsira E, Fournet F, Moiroux N. Investigating the role of urban vegetation alongside other environmental variables in shaping Aedes albopictus presence and abundance in Montpellier, France. PLoS One. 2025;20(11):e0335793.
notes: Confirmed. Above 23% the curve flattens; it does not show a decline. Local result, not a general threshold; for Greek cities it can only illustrate the idea.

value_text: Optional context — modelled dengue-transmission potential (R0) by Ae. albopictus: peak 26.4 °C (95% CI 25.2–27.4), zero below 16.2 °C (13.2–19.9) and above 31.6 °C (29.4–33.7).
context: Mechanistic R0(T) model built from Bayesian thermal-response fits to published laboratory trait data (mosquito traits plus DENV infection traits), validated against human case data in the Americas.
quote: transmission peaked at 26.4°C (95% CI: 25.2–27.4°C) and declined to zero below 16.2°C
citation: Mordecai EA, Cohen JM, Evans MV, Gudapati P, Johnson LR, Lippi CA, et al. Detecting the impact of temperature on transmission of Zika, dengue, and chikungunya using mechanistic models. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2017;11(4):e0005568.
notes: Exact numbers confirmed in the results (upper limit 31.6 °C, 95% CI 29.4–33.7). These are limits for modelled transmission potential, NOT for mosquito survival or activity, because R0 also contains virus traits (infection probability, extrinsic incubation). For a mosquito-only temperature curve see item 15. The paper states that the mosquito traits peak between 23 and 34 °C for the two species. A 2022 correction (PLoS Negl Trop Dis 16(6):e0010514) concerns supplementary figures L–M and one supplementary paragraph, not these main-text values.

value_text: Optional context — fitted thermal limits (T0 = lower, Tm = upper, posterior mean °C) of Ae. albopictus traits: biting rate 10.25 / 38.32; eggs per female per gonotrophic cycle 8.02 / 35.65; egg-to-adult survival 9.04 / 39.33; egg-to-adult development rate 8.60 / 39.66; adult lifespan 13.41 / 31.51.
context: Supporting Information S2 Text, Table A of Mordecai et al. 2017: Bayesian Brière or quadratic fits to laboratory data compiled from several studies; mean and 95% credible (HPD) intervals of the critical thermal minimum T0 and maximum Tm of each fitted curve.
quote: Paraphrase: Table A gives mean and 95% CI of T0 and Tm per trait
citation: Mordecai EA, Cohen JM, Evans MV, Gudapati P, Johnson LR, Lippi CA, et al. Detecting the impact of temperature on transmission of Zika, dengue, and chikungunya using mechanistic models. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2017;11(4):e0005568. Supporting Information S2 Text, Table A.
notes: T0/Tm are where each FITTED curve reaches zero (extrapolated from constant-temperature lab data), not observed death limits; credible intervals are wide. The optima under 'derived_optimum_not_printed_in_source' were computed by us from the posterior-mean T0 and Tm (quadratic: (T0+Tm)/2; Brière: positive root of 5T² − (4Tm+3T0)T + 2T0·Tm = 0); they are approximations and do not appear in the paper. Adult lifespan has the lowest upper limit (31.5 °C, close to the R0 upper limit of 31.6 °C); the S1 Text states that R0 is strongly limited by short mosquito lifespans at high temperatures and that lifespan drives the difference between the Ae. albopictus and Ae. aegypti R0 curves.
